query: Refractory high-entropy alloys are promising structural materials, but achieving a strong combination of strength and plasticity remains important. What single intervention could improve this strength–plasticity combination? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, its expected mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an appropriate reference alloy, the conditions under which it should hold, supporting evidence from prior studies, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing controlled interstitial carbon into a refractory high‐entropy alloy (e.g., NbMoTaW‐based) will activate transformation-induced plasticity (TRIP) mechanisms that simultaneously enhance yield strength and ductility compared to the undoped baseline.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventional refractory high-entropy alloy without interstitial carbon, typically exhibiting high strength but limited ductility due to brittle behavior.
generation.intervention: Add a controlled, low-to-moderate amount of interstitial carbon during alloy processing.
generation.conditions: This improvement is expected under standard room temperature deformation conditions and typical processing routes that avoid excessive formation of brittle carbide phases. The carbon content must be optimized to trigger TRIP without promoting severe carbide precipitation.
generation.structural_mediator: The interstitial carbon is anticipated to occupy lattice sites and locally distort the matrix, thereby promoting a phase transformation (martensitic transformation) that acts as a TRIP mechanism. The resulting in situ formation of a secondary phase along with nano-twinning should serve as an additional active deformation mode.
generation.mechanism: The addition of carbon induces localized lattice strain, which triggers a martensitic transformation during mechanical loading. This TRIP effect works in concert with traditional dislocation slip, enhancing strain hardening and delaying the onset of localized necking, thereby overcoming the typical strength–ductility trade-off in refractory HEAs.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline alloy, the carbon-doped alloy will demonstrate a statistically significant increase in both yield strength and tensile ductility. Although the exact magnitude is uncertain, improvements should be observable in standard tensile tests (e.g., higher elongation to failure combined with increased strength).
generation.baseline: Refractory HEA without interstitial carbon addition, exhibiting high strength but limited plasticity.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to refractory HEAs where carbon can be homogeneously dissolved interstitially without forming excessive, brittle carbide precipitates. Deviations in processing conditions or carbon content that favor undesirable carbide formation may invalidate the improvement.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal carbon content and processing parameters to achieve the TRIP effect without excessive carbide precipitation are not precisely defined. There is also uncertainty regarding the universality of the effect across different refractory HEA compositions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of refractory HEA samples: one serving as the control (no carbon) and one with a precisely controlled amount of interstitial carbon. Process both sets identically. Carry out standard tensile tests at room temperature along with detailed microstructural analysis (using X-ray diffraction, electron microscopy, and electron backscatter diffraction) to examine phase evolution and TRIP activation during deformation.
measurements: Yield strength and ultimate tensile strength
Identification of TRIP-induced phases or nano-twins via microscopy and XRD
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the carbon-doped samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in the combination of strength and ductility relative to the control or if the microstructural analysis fails to demonstrate evidence of TRIP activity (or shows detrimental carbide formation leading to embrittlement), then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: With the development of high-temperature metallic materials, Ni-based superalloys have been unable to meet the requirements of aerospace engines. It is urgent to find a new high-performance alloy to replace the Ni-based superalloy []. Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) based on refractory elements with superior high-temperature mechanical properties have recently attracted intensive research attention, which are regarded as promising candidates for high-temperature structural materials [,,]. However, their inferior plasticity along with high ductile–brittle transition temperature and high density seriously limits their aerospace applications, where the requirements are mainly focus on the deformability and high specific strength of alloys.

Research efforts have been attempting to overcoming these shortcomings via component and structure regulation [,]. In order to improve plasticity at room temperature (RT), a new refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA), HfNbTaTiZr [], with excellent RT compression plasticity (ε > 50%), has been developed. However, its specific yield strength (SYS) at high temperatures is undesirability (such as <60 MPa·cm3/g at 1073 K). For better SYS, Han et al. [] and Wang et al. [] added Ti or V to NbMoTaW and NbMoTa RHEAs, respectively. Unfortunately, their SYSs are still lower than 90 MPa·cm3/g at 1073 K. Hence, the harmonization of strength, plasticity, and density is an intractable problem in RHEAs. Meanwhile, the strain softening phenomenon in RHEAs at high temperatures is ubiquitous, but the quantitative analysis of the softening mechanism is still lacking [,,,].

This research systematically studies the Fe-Co-Cr-Ni-Mo-C-based medium-entropy alloy’s mechanical properties and microstructure at R.T., 77 K, and 4.2 K. The mechanisms of micro-defect activation during deformation under cryogenic conditions are the main concern. The main findings can be summarized as follows: FeCoCrNiMo5−xCx-based alloys exhibit outstanding mechanical properties under cryogenic conditions. Particularly for the Mo4C1 alloy, the strength and ductility increase simultaneously from R.T. to 4.2 K. The tensile strength and elongation of the Mo4C1 alloy are 776 MPa and 50.5% at R.T., 1418 MPa and 71.2% in liquid nitrogen 77 K, and 1670 MPa and 80.0% in liquid helium 4.2 K, respectively. Under the R.T. condition, the primary contributing mechanism of strain hardening is twinning-induced plasticity. At 77 K and 4.2 K, the activation of martensitic transformation to partially replace the twining mechanism (TRIP) became the main reason for plasticity improvement during cryogenic tensile deformation. High-entropy alloys (HEAs), or multi-principal-element alloys, emerge as a new research frontier in the metallic materials community. HEAs differentiate with conventional alloys in that they have at least four principal elements, instead of one or two in the latter. It is a breakthrough to the alloy design in the traditional physical metallurgy, and it opens a new arena for explorations of new materials and new properties. Previous studies have indicated that HEAs have a high softening resistance at elevated temperatures, and sluggish diffusion kinetics. Therefore, HEAs are widely regarded as highly promising high-temperature materials. Before the high-temperature application of HEAs can be seriously pursued, a technical challenge in terms of the mechanical property needs to be tackled. Basically, single-phased HEAs have been found difficult to reach a reasonable balance between strength and (tensile) ductility. Single-phased fcc structured HEAs are ductile but not strong enough. Single-phased bcc structured HEAs, on the other hand, can be very strong but at the price of brittleness. reading.lever: Introduce controlled interstitial carbon to refractory HEAs to activate TRIP, unifying strengthening mechanisms.
reading.why: Evidence from TRIP-DP HEAs shows that interstitial carbon can trigger phase transformation plasticity, potentially overcoming the strength–ductility trade-off in refractory HEAs.
